Check that the @names in a message belon: Check that the @names in a message belong to real Twitch accounts. Bots like to mention names that don't exist, so a made-up name adds suspicion.
Catch links broken up with spaces or ext: Catch links broken up with spaces or extra dots to slip past link detection, like "twitch. tv" or "example . com".
Catch strings that look like gift or vou: Catch strings that look like gift or voucher codes, such as "GVP-8IJN-VV65-8QWG". "Free viewers" scams use them a lot.
Turn the whole Spam Learner module on or: Turn the whole Spam Learner module on or off. While it is off, nothing new gets suggested or added, and you are left with the keywords and patterns already in your lists.
Post in chat when the learner writes new: Post in chat when the learner writes new suggestions or promotes one on its own.
Let the learner move well-proven suggest:
Let the learner move well-proven suggestions into the active rule list (spam.json) on its own, without asking you.
Every new find starts as a pending suggestion. It is only marked "trusted" and promoted once it has proven itself often enough; the thresholds below set how often.
Clean out learner data that has gone sta:
Clean out learner data that has gone stale.
Active spam rules and pending suggestions are checked against the most recent violations and removed once they stop turning up.
Protect the entries you added to spam.js:
Protect the entries you added to spam.json by hand (they start with "!") from the automatic cleanup.
Turn this off only if decay may remove everything, your own rules included.
Turn the whole AutoMod module on or off.
Also let TwitchSentry approve or deny Au: Also let TwitchSentry approve or deny AutoMod-held messages from accounts that Twitch already restricts or monitors.
Turn the whole Check Link module on or o: Turn the whole Check Link module on or off.
Remember each link's scan result for a w:
Remember each link's scan result for a while, so the same link posted again is answered from memory instead of costing another API call.
This is what keeps a raid affordable: thirty accounts pasting one link is one scan, not thirty. Every one of those messages is still deleted and still gets its notification — only the lookup is skipped.
Turn this off only if you want every single post re-scanned live.
How long a remembered scan result stays:
How long a remembered scan result stays usable before the link is scanned again.
Shorter means a site that gets compromised is re-checked sooner; longer means fewer API calls.
60 minutes is a good balance — a raid arrives inside a few minutes, so even a short window catches it, while an hour keeps a busy chat well inside the daily quota.
How many links in one message TwitchSent:
How many links in one message TwitchSentry scans before it stops and ignores the rest.
Every scan costs one call against your API quota (VirusTotal's free tier allows 4 per minute and 500 per day), and a link the scanner has never seen takes around 20 seconds to come back.
Without a cap, one message stuffed with links can spend the whole day's quota and hold up moderation while it is worked through.
3 is plenty for normal conversation. Raise it only if people in your chat really do post several links at once.
Rewrite links in the bot's own scan mess:
Rewrite links in the bot's own scan messages so they cannot be clicked — "example.com" is posted as "example[.]com".
The bot is a moderator, so nothing filters what it says. Repeating a malicious link back into chat, right after deleting the message that carried it, hands it out again from an account viewers trust.
Turn this off only if you would rather the links stayed clickable.
Post in chat when a scanned link comes b: Post in chat when a scanned link comes back suspicious: not confirmed dangerous, but worth being careful with.
Post in chat when a scanned link is conf: Post in chat when a scanned link is confirmed malicious.
Post in chat when a link is too new or t: Post in chat when a link is too new or too obscure for the scanners to know anything about it.
Post in chat when a scan could not finis: Post in chat when a scan could not finish, for example because the scanning service was slow or down.
Also scan links with IPQualityScore (IPQ: Also scan links with IPQualityScore (IPQS) for a second opinion next to VirusTotal. It is especially good at spotting brand-new throwaway phishing domains.
Turn the whole Voting module on or off.
Post in chat how a vote is going: when i: Post in chat how a vote is going: when it starts, how it stands and how it ends.
Ban the target of a successful vote inst: Ban the target of a successful vote instead of the default timeout.
Never let a vote succeed against one of: Never let a vote succeed against one of your subscribers.
Never let a vote succeed against someone: Never let a vote succeed against someone with the VIP badge.
How old an account must be, in days, bef:
How old an account must be, in days, before it no longer counts as new.
A younger account makes everything else the message trips count for more ('New Account Risk Factor'); with 'Act On Account Age Alone' on, it adds its own score instead.
(Example: 30 = accounts less than 30 days old count as new)
How many emotes a message needs before t:
How many emotes a message needs before the emote-share check looks at it at all.
Messages with fewer emotes are always left alone by that check.
How many emotes in a row (with no words:
How many emotes in a row (with no words between them) it takes to count as spam.
Example: 5 = five or more emotes back-to-back adds to the score.
How many letters a message needs before:
How many letters a message needs before the caps check looks at it.
This keeps short messages like "LOL" from being flagged just for being in capitals.
How many times the exact same character:
How many times the exact same character has to repeat in a row to count as character spam.
Example: 6 = something like "AAAAAA" or "!!!!!!" (6 or more in a row) adds to the score.
Sliding time window in which a user's me:
Sliding time window in which a user's messages are counted.
(Example: 10 = only messages from the last 10 seconds count toward the velocity check)
Maximum number of messages a user may se:
Maximum number of messages a user may send within the window.
Sending more than this triggers a score hit.
(Example: 5 = the 6th message within the window triggers)
Sliding time window in which repeated me:
Sliding time window in which repeated messages are compared.
Older messages expire and no longer count as duplicates.
How many identical or similar messages (:
How many identical or similar messages (the current one included) it takes within the window to trigger a score hit.
(Example: 3 = posting the same thing a third time triggers)
Minimum message length (letters/digits a:
Minimum message length (letters/digits after normalization) for the duplicate check.
Short messages like 'gg' or 'lol' are ignored — repeated short messages are still caught by the velocity check.
How long the raid protection stays armed:
How long the raid protection stays armed after an incoming raid.
After this duration the module goes back to sleep until the next raid.
Only arm the protection for raids with a:
Only arm the protection for raids with at least this many viewers.
(Example: 0 = arm on every raid; 20 = ignore small friendly raids)
Sliding time window in which a user's me: Sliding time window in which a user's messages are counted during the raid window.
Maximum number of messages a user may se: Maximum number of messages a user may send within the window during a raid.
Sliding time window in which repeated me: Sliding time window in which repeated messages of the same user are compared.
Number of identical or similar messages:
Number of identical or similar messages from the same user within the window required to trigger.
(Example: 2 = the first repetition already triggers)
Minimum message length (letters/digits a:
Minimum message length (letters/digits after normalization) for the duplicate and swarm checks.
Shorter messages are only covered by the velocity check.
Sliding time window in which messages fr: Sliding time window in which messages from different users are compared against each other.

Only Act On Known Spam Wording: Only Act On Known Spam Wording
The minimum number of different accounts:
The minimum number of different accounts that must post near-identical messages within the window. The share below can raise this number, never lower it.
(Example: 5 = the fifth account posting the wave message turns it into a coordinated swarm, as long as the wording is on a spam list)
The same bar as a share of the viewers t:
The same bar as a share of the viewers the raid brought. The check uses whichever is larger: this share or the count above.
Three accounts posting the same line are most of a raid of four, and nothing at all in a raid of nine hundred. A fixed number can't mean the same in both.
0 turns the share off and leaves only the fixed count. Ignored when Twitch sent no viewer count with the raid.
What a message adds to the score just fo:
What a message adds to the score just for matching this channel's spam lists, whether or not anyone else posted it.
On its own it is not enough: a single spammy message is the Spam Filter's job. Together with a swarm or a repeat, it is what makes Raid Protection act.
How long (in seconds) a timeout lasts wh: How long (in seconds) a timeout lasts when "Action On Violation" above is set to Timeout. Example: 600 = 10 minutes.
How long (in seconds) the escalation tim: How long (in seconds) the escalation timeout lasts. Example: 60 = 1 minute.
After this many hours without a new viol: After this many hours without a new violation, a viewer's warning count goes back to zero, so a warning from weeks ago doesn't count against them forever.
How long (in seconds) a permit lasts by: How long (in seconds) a permit lasts by default when a moderator grants one. Example: 120 = 2 minutes.
The longest permit anyone can hand out. A moderator who types a longer time in "!Permit @user 3000" gets this instead, and so does a default or self-permit duration set above it.
This is what stops a mistyped duration from switching moderation off for someone for hours. Capped at 86400 (24 hours) whatever you put here.
Several viewers can hold a permit at the: Several viewers can hold a permit at the same time, each with its own countdown. A permit that is already running is never extended — !Permit for someone who already has one is refused, so end it with "!EndPermit @user" first. "!EndPermit" with no name ends every active permit at once.
Set the reward up on Twitch with \"Skip:
Set the reward up on Twitch with "Skip Reward Requests Queue" turned OFF. That is what lets TwitchSentry give the points back when a redemption cannot become a permit — the viewer already has one, or the feature is off. A reward that skips the queue is spent the moment it is redeemed and Twitch will not allow a refund.
Point the reward's Streamer.bot trigger at this same Permit action.
How long (in seconds) a self-granted per: How long (in seconds) a self-granted permit lasts. Example: 120 = 2 minutes.
How many hours the learner keeps its dow:
How many hours the learner keeps its downloaded list of everyday words (in many languages) before fetching it again. The list stops ordinary words like "the" or "und" from ever being suggested as spam.
Higher = fewer downloads. Lower = a fresher list, though that is rarely needed: it barely changes.

How many hours the learner keeps its downloaded list of valid domain endings (.com, .net and so on) before fetching it again.
Higher = fewer downloads. Lower = a fresher list, which is rarely needed.
How many different people must have post:
How many different people must have posted something before it can become a suggestion at all.
That way one persistent spammer can't teach the learner a new rule alone. Real spam campaigns usually use more than one account.
The minimum \"confidence score\" somethi:
The minimum "confidence score" something needs before it's written down as a suggestion for you to review.
Confidence is a combined score based on how often it showed up, how many different messages and people it came from, and how spam-like the message around it looked.
The minimum confidence score a suggestio:
The minimum confidence score a suggestion needs to become "trusted" and be eligible for auto-promotion into spam.json.
Only matters if "Auto Promote Trusted Rules" above is turned on.
In how many separate learner runs a sugg:
In how many separate learner runs a suggestion must turn up again before it can be promoted automatically.
This makes sure it is a real, recurring pattern and not a one-off before it becomes an active rule.
The minimum number of times something mu:
The minimum number of times something must show up (weighted) in recent violations before the learner considers it at all.
This is only a first filter. It still has to meet the other requirements (how many messages, how many different people, and confidence) before it becomes a suggestion.
In how many separate violation-log entri:
In how many separate violation-log entries something must appear before it can be suggested.
This keeps a single, very repetitive spam message from teaching the learner a new rule on its own.
Higher = more cautious and slower. Lower = reacts sooner, on less evidence.
The most single-word keyword suggestions:
The most single-word keyword suggestions the learner may add or refresh in one run.
A cap, so one busy run can't flood your suggestions list.
The most two-word phrase suggestions the:
The most two-word phrase suggestions the learner may add or refresh in one run.
Phrases tend to be more precise than single keywords.
The most new domain-ending (TLD) suggest: The most new domain-ending (TLD) suggestions the learner may add or refresh in one run, taken from spaced-out or disguised links it spotted.
How many of the latest lines in violatio:
How many of the latest lines in violation-log.txt the learner reads each time it looks for new patterns.
More lines give it more history to learn from and usually better results, but each run takes a little longer.
How much extra weight the message that s:
How much extra weight the message that started this run gets compared to older messages in the history.
Higher = the newest violation counts for more in this run, but it still has to meet the same requirements as everything else to become a suggestion.
How hard a word is penalised when it als:
How hard a word is penalised when it also shows up a lot in ordinary chat (see "Clean-Chat Sample Rate" below).
Lower = stricter: everyday words from normal chat are held back harder, which avoids false alarms such as suggesting "google".
TwitchSentry saves about 1 in every N or:
TwitchSentry saves about 1 in every N ordinary chat messages to clean-log.txt to build a sample of what everyday chat looks like. The Clean Penalty Divisor above works from this sample.
Higher = samples less often and keeps the file smaller. Lower = builds the sample faster, but writes to disk more often.
In how many separate learner runs a new:
In how many separate learner runs a new suggestion must keep turning up before it moves from "probation" to "trusted".
Higher = slower but safer. Lower = faster, on less evidence.
How many learner runs a pending suggesti:
How many learner runs a pending suggestion may go without turning up again before it is removed from the suggestions list.
This gives suggestions some slack, so a short quiet spell doesn't wipe them out right away.
How many of the most recent violation-lo: How many of the most recent violation-log entries are checked when deciding what still counts as "active" during cleanup.
How many times a rule or suggestion has:
How many times a rule or suggestion has to show up within that recent window to count as still active and be kept.
Higher = cleans up more aggressively. Lower = keeps rarely-used patterns around longer.
The lowest AutoMod level TwitchSentry ac:
The lowest AutoMod level TwitchSentry acts on. Twitch rates every held message from 1 to 4; a message rated below this level is left for a moderator to decide.
Lower = TwitchSentry handles more held messages. Higher = only those Twitch rates higher.
IPQS rates every link from 0 (safe) to 1:
IPQS rates every link from 0 (safe) to 100 (certainly malicious). This is the score from which TwitchSentry treats a link as a threat.
At 75 a link counts as suspicious; such links often belong to a proxy, a VPN exit node or a known bad actor.
IPQS itself recommends 85 for blocking outright and 75 for flagging for review, so 75 is the more cautious default.
Raise it toward 90 if your channel sees too many false alarms.
A lower, stricter version of the thresho:
A lower, stricter version of the threshold above, used only when IPQS also reports the domain as recently registered, that is, a brand-new website.
Throwaway domains are a common phishing trick: register one, use it once, abandon it.
Because a new domain is riskier from the start, a fraud score as low as 40 (normally "low risk") already triggers a warning here.
Set it higher (for example 60-70) to give new domains more benefit of the doubt.
How long (in seconds) the timeout lasts: How long (in seconds) the timeout lasts when a vote succeeds. Example: 1800 = 30 minutes.
How many different viewers need to vote: How many different viewers need to vote before the vote succeeds and action is taken.
How long a vote stays open for new votes: How long a vote stays open for new votes to count. If this runs out before enough votes come in, the vote resets and has to start over.
What percentage of the message needs to:
What percentage of the message needs to be emotes before it counts as emote spam. Enter this as a fraction of 1 (0.6 = 60%).
Example: 0.6 = a message that's more than 60% emotes adds to the score.
What percentage of the message's letters:
What percentage of the message's letters need to be UPPERCASE before it counts as caps spam. Enter this as a fraction of 1 (0.65 = 65%).
Example: 0.65 = a message where more than 65% of its letters are capitals adds to the score.
How similar two messages must be to coun:
How similar two messages must be to count as duplicates, from 0.0 to 1.0.
1.0 = only exact matches; 0.85 = small edits like added characters or swapped words still match.
Lower values catch more variations but risk false positives.
Total score the checks must add up to be:
Total score the checks must add up to before Message Filter acts.
(Example: 1.5 = a single hit at its default weight reaches it; whether one hit on its own is enough depends on 'Require Two Signals')
Score added when a viewer sends more mes: Score added when a viewer sends more messages than the window allows.
How similar two messages must be to coun:
How similar two messages must be to count as duplicates, from 0.0 to 1.0.
Slightly looser than Message Filter's flood check by default, since raid bots often change a few characters at random.
Score added when a viewer repeats the sa: Score added when a viewer repeats the same message too often.
Score added on a swarm hit.\nAt the defa:
Score added on a swarm hit.
At the default of 1.5 a swarm alone stays below the default threshold of 2.0; together with the spam wording hit (1.0) it is acted on.
Total score that must be reached across: Total score that must be reached across all checks before action is taken.
What percentage of the message needs to:
What percentage of the message needs to be emotes before it counts as emote spam during a raid. Enter this as a fraction of 1 (0.65 = 65%).
Example: 0.65 = a message that's more than 65% emotes adds to the score.
What percentage of the message's letters:
What percentage of the message's letters need to be UPPERCASE before it counts as caps spam during a raid. Enter this as a fraction of 1 (0.65 = 65%).
Example: 0.65 = a message where more than 65% of its letters are capitals adds to the score.
Covered up by default, so the window is: Covered up by default, so the window is safe to have on screen. Click the eye to uncover a value, or paste a new one straight into the dots with Ctrl+V — you never have to uncover a field just to replace it.
Show this value. It covers itself again: Show this value. It covers itself again as soon as you click away, and every time the window is opened. You can also paste a new one straight into the dots with Ctrl+V.
Domain endings (like \"xyz\" or \"gg\"): Domain endings (like "xyz" or "gg") TwitchSentry looks for when someone disguises a link with added spaces or dots, as in "streamboo .gg".
Text patterns (regex or plain text) for:
Text patterns (regex or plain text) for spam a simple word list can't catch, such as keyboard mash, disguised phrases or lookalike characters. One pattern per line.
(No regex experience? Plain words and phrases work too, they are just less flexible than a full pattern.)
Patterns for text shaped like a gift cod: Patterns for text shaped like a gift code, serial key or promo code (like "XXXX-XXXX-XXXX"). A match counts as promo-code evidence on its own, whether or not the message also matched a keyword.
Words or phrases that always go through,:
Words or phrases that always go through, even when Twitch's AutoMod flags them.
Mostly useful in non-English chats, where AutoMod sometimes mistakes ordinary words for something harmful.
Usernames that can never be voted agains: Usernames that can never be voted against. One per line.
Like \"Excluded Users\", but for whole S: Like "Excluded Users", but for whole Streamer.bot user groups, which you manage in Streamer.bot's "Users" section.

Sent when a user's account is younger th: Sent when a user's account is younger than 'Min. Account Age'.
Sent when a message has too high an emot: Sent when a message has too high an emote-to-word ratio or too many consecutive emotes.
Sent when a user exceeds the message vel: Sent when a user exceeds the message velocity limit.
Sent when a user repeats the same or sim: Sent when a user repeats the same or similar message too often.

Posted in chat after someone is timed ou: Posted in chat after someone is timed out for this.

Posted in chat when a link is merely sus: Posted in chat when a link is merely suspicious. The original message is deleted first, just to be safe.
Posted in chat when a link scans clean.
Posted in chat when a link is too new or: Posted in chat when a link is too new or too obscure for the scan to return a result.
Posted in chat if a scan couldn't finish: Posted in chat if a scan couldn't finish for any reason.
Whispered back when someone sends the bo:
Whispered back when someone sends the bot a link but no scanning service is set up: no VirusTotal key, or IPQS turned on without its key.

Posted in chat when a new vote begins.

Posted in chat if a moderator manually c: Posted in chat if a moderator manually cancels a vote before it finishes.

Only act when a message contains at least two different parts of an advert.
This is the single most important protection against deleting real conversation. "I got 100 followers today" is an Offer and nothing else, so it is left alone. "100 followers free, join discord.gg/x" is an Offer plus a Destination, so it is not.

"Real" means: seen chatting here recently, or (with "Verify Mentioned Users" on) an existing Twitch account. Example: 0.5 = someone greeting three regulars is left alone.
